title: The Crucifixion and Resurrection of Jesus
lead: The greatest defeat turns out to be the greatest victory. Death does not get the last word.
questions: What in my life looks finished for good, and what would it mean to trust that God writes the next chapter after the words “The End”?
What does my waiting look like on the silent Sabbath: what do I do in the stretch of time when nothing is happening and I simply have to stay faithful?
What changes in me when I realize that the risen Lord began not with crowds or proofs, but by speaking a single name, including mine?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: The last stretch of our journey is called “There Is Hope When the End Turns Out to Be a Beginning,” and it opens with the event this whole series has been heading toward since Eden: the offspring of the woman crushes the serpent’s head at the cost of a wounded heel. The Gospels describe the execution itself in a handful of words, “they crucified Him there,” with no attempt to shock; we only learn about the nails when the risen Lord shows His hands. But Luke recorded something unheard of at an execution: the condemned man’s first words are a prayer for his executioners. “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And the criminal hanging beside Him, a man who can no longer do anything at all, make amends or sign up for any community, asks only, “Jesus, remember me,” and hears, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Salvation by grace has its purest test case up there on Golgotha.

John remembered a word from the cross, tetelestai, “It is finished”: the word used to mark a bill as paid. The temple curtain was torn down the middle. And between Friday and Sunday there is one more day we rarely talk about: the women had prepared spices, but “they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.” It was faithfulness to the commandment that set the calendar of Easter morning: Sunday was simply the first morning they could go. The rhythm of God’s commandments turned out to carry the greatest news in history.

The empty tomb was discovered by women, though no court of the day would have accepted their testimony; that is not how anyone invents a legend. To the apostles their words “seemed like nonsense.” Peter ran, stooped at the low entrance, and saw something more eloquent than emptiness: the linen cloths lying there and the head cloth rolled up separately. A thief doesn’t unwrap a body and fold the bedding. And Mary Magdalene, weeping outside the tomb, recognized the risen Lord not by His face but by one word: “Mary.” The sheep know the voice of the Shepherd who calls them by name. He sent her to “My brothers”: the very men who had failed and run away were, after the resurrection, called brothers for the first time.

On Friday evening the case of Jesus was closed, with all the evidence in. That very end turned out to be the beginning of everything. God has a habit of writing the next chapter after the words “The End.”

Today we begin the last stretch of our journey: “There Is Hope When the End Turns Out to Be a Beginning.” And we begin with the event this whole series has been heading toward since day one. In Eden came the promise that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent’s head, but would pay for it with a wounded heel. For thirty-five days we have watched that promise travel through history: through the flood and the Red Sea, through Bethlehem and Bethany. Today the bill comes due. The price turns out to be a cross, and the payment is made over one long weekend, from Friday afternoon to Sunday dawn.

sections.heading: Father, Forgive Them
paragraphs: It is striking how little space the Gospels give to the execution itself. The passion narratives are long and detailed, but at the moment everything has been building toward, the text simply says: “they crucified Him there, along with the criminals.” A handful of words, nothing sensational. The evangelists are not writing for effect; we don’t even hear about the nails until after the resurrection, when Jesus shows His hands. But Luke recorded something that never happened at executions: the condemned man’s first words are a prayer for his executioners. “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” The preacher who spent three years teaching people to love their enemies does exactly what He taught in His hour of trial, at a moment when no one would have blamed Him for screaming. And it happened in public in the most literal sense: Rome crucified people along busy roads because, as one Roman teacher of rhetoric wrote, the punishment was meant to deter the widest possible audience. Golgotha lay just outside the city wall, beside a road full of passersby. So the first prayer for the forgiveness of murderers was not spoken in a chapel but beside a busy highway, in full view of everyone the empire wanted to teach fear. Above His head hangs a sign with the charge: “This is the King of the Jews.” The chief priests demanded that Pilate correct it: let him write that this man only claimed to be king. Pilate refused. The irony of that sign runs two ways, because, as we saw two days ago, “king” was the one title Jesus never used of Himself, and He slipped away from the crowd that wanted to crown Him. He died with someone else’s accusation over His head, and it was the truest sentence written anywhere in that whole trial.

sections.heading: Today You Will Be with Me
paragraphs: Two criminals hang on either side of Him, and among the three crosses plays out a scene that alone would make Luke’s account worth keeping. One of the condemned men mocks. The other does something astonishing: he defends the innocent one, admits his own guilt, and asks, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!” A man nailed to a beam can no longer do anything: he can’t make amends, can’t turn over a new leaf, can’t sign up for any community. All he has left is his voice and his last breaths. And he hears: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” In the thinking of the day, a crucified criminal belonged in the column of the ungodly, bound for eternal rejection. With one sentence Jesus moves him from that column to the other one, among the righteous, and into the best company imaginable: “with Me.” The last person Jesus won before He died was a condemned man with no merits at all, baptized only by his own confession. Salvation by grace through faith has its purest test case right there, up on Golgotha.

sections.heading: It Is Finished
paragraphs: John remembered words from the cross as short as a breath, because the mechanics of crucifixion allowed nothing longer. “I am thirsty”: the one who promised the Samaritan woman living water dies thirsty. And then a single Greek word, tetelestai: “It is finished.” Not “it’s over,” not “I’ve lost,” but done, carried through to the goal, paid in full. In that world, this was the word used to mark a bill as settled. At the moment of His death, the evangelists note, the temple curtain was torn down the middle: the veil that separated people from the Most Holy Place ceased to exist, as if someone had flung the doors of the house wide open. A Roman centurion, a professional witness to hundreds of executions, says, “Surely this was a righteous man.” And the crowd that had come as if to a show goes home “beating their breasts.” No one understands yet what has happened. But everyone senses this was no ordinary execution. John adds a detail to the scene, and for once he interrupts his narrative to testify that he saw it with his own eyes: from the side pierced by the spear came blood and water. Doctors recognize in this description fluid from the sac around the heart mixed with blood, the sign of a death that had really taken place. The evangelist knew nothing of that medicine; he simply wrote down what he saw, and that is exactly why his note is worth so much.

sections.heading: The Sabbath
paragraphs: Between Friday and Sunday the Gospels record a day we rarely talk about. The women, who had watched their Teacher die from a distance, prepared spices. “And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.” On the darkest Saturday in history, with their hearts broken to pieces, the women who followed Jesus did what they did every week: they rested for the LORD. And He Himself, who on Friday had said “It is finished,” lay at rest in the tomb the whole Sabbath long, like the Creator who rested on the seventh day after His finished work. And it was faithfulness to the commandment that set the calendar of Easter morning: the women did not go to the tomb on Saturday, not because they lacked the strength, but because they were keeping the Sabbath. The first day of the week was simply the first day they could go. The rhythm of God’s commandments turned out to carry the greatest news in history.

sections.heading: He Is Not Here
paragraphs: Sunday morning begins with women, and that is the first thing nobody would have made up. In that world a woman’s testimony carried no weight in court; Josephus says plainly that the testimony of women is not to be accepted. Anyone inventing a resurrection legend would have had respected men discover the empty tomb. The Gospels give first place to the very people that world didn’t believe, because that is how it happened; and the apostles themselves reacted just as the times would lead you to expect: “their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women.” John’s account holds one more small detail of this kind: although he mentions only Mary Magdalene at the tomb, he leaves the plural in her mouth: “we do not know where they have put Him!” It is an unintended trace of the other women we know from the other Gospels. A forger would have made the numbers match; a witness writes it down the way it was said. Peter ran to check. The entrances to tombs in those days were low, about the height of a crouching person, so the Gospels note the whole awkward maneuver precisely: he bent down, looked in, saw. And what he saw was more eloquent than emptiness: the linen cloths lying there and the cloth from His head rolled up separately, in its own place. A grave robber doesn’t unwrap a body from its linens and fold up the head cloth. The tomb did not look robbed. It looked like someone had left it and put away the bedding on the way out.

sections.heading: Mary!
paragraphs: John saved the most beautiful scene of that morning for last. Mary Magdalene stands outside the tomb, weeping; even angels make no impression on her, because she isn’t looking for angels, only for the body of her Lord. Behind her she hears a question: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” She takes Him for the gardener. And then comes one word: “Mary.” Not a lecture on the resurrection, not a proof, not a rebuke. Her name. She recognized Him not by His face and not by His wounds, but by the way He said her name, and it would be hard to find a more beautiful illustration of what this Gospel said earlier: “the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name.” The risen Lord sends her off with a message: “Go and tell My brothers.” Brothers. John quietly records a promotion: in his book these same men were first disciples, then friends, and now, after the resurrection, after they had all failed and run away, they are called brothers for the first time. The cross didn’t just pay the bills. It made a family. And the first person sent out with the news of the resurrection was a woman whose testimony no court of that world would have accepted. With God, the witnesses the world didn’t count have counted from the very beginning.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: The stretch we begin today is called “when the end turns out to be a beginning,” and the Easter weekend is the pattern for that sentence forever. On Friday evening the case of Jesus was closed in every possible sense: the leader executed, the disciples scattered, hope buried and sealed behind a stone. All the facts lined up; no one had any illusions. And yet this very end, sealed like no other, turned out to be the beginning of everything. If you are carrying a Friday inside you today, a closed case, lost with all the evidence in, this story tells you: God has a habit of writing the next chapter after the words “The End.” He doesn’t promise there will be no Friday, or no dark Saturday when nothing happens and you simply have to hold on faithfully, like those women. He promises Sunday. And one more thing: the risen Lord did not start with crowds or with proofs for skeptics. He started by speaking one name. That is exactly how the gospel spreads through the world, from person to person, by name, and your name, too, has already been spoken in that garden.
